passage_1: "A Multidisciplinary Approach to the Adolescent Bariatric Surgical Patient" evaluates the establishment, early outcomes, and multidisciplinary framework of a pediatric bariatric surgery program—specifically the Comprehensive Weight Management Center at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center—for treating clinically severe obesity in adolescents. Examining referrals and initial surgical cases using Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGBP), the study found that RYGBP leads to significant, clinically meaningful weight loss and the reversal of severe comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea, though medical and behavioral complications can occur. The paper recommends managing adolescent bariatric surgery within a comprehensive, multidisciplinary team of pediatric specialists to address the unique medical, developmental, and psychosocial needs of young patients. Furthermore, it outlines clinical guidelines requiring candidates to have achieved most of their linear growth, have a BMI ≥40 with severe comorbidities or a BMI ≥50 with less severe comorbidities, and demonstrate the ability to commit to lifelong medical surveillance and dietary supplementation.
passage_2: "Teen-Longitudinal Assessment of Bariatric Surgery (Teen-LABS): Methodologic Features of the First Prospective Multicenter Study of Adolescent Bariatric Surgery" evaluates the methodological design and protocol of the first prospective, multicenter observational study designed to collect coordinated clinical, epidemiological, and behavioral data on adolescents (≤19 years old) undergoing bariatric surgery compared to adult historical counterparts. The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.

The study findings demonstrate that gastrointestinal metabolic surgery achieves superior, durable glycemic control and significant reduction of cardiovascular risk factors compared to standard medical interventions. Based on these insights, the guidelines recommend metabolic surgery as a standard treatment option for T2D in candidates with class III obesity BMI≥40 kg/m² regardless of glycemic control, as well as for patients with class II obesity BMI 35.0-39.9 kg/m² when hyperglycemia is inadequately controlled by optimal medical therapy. Additionally, the guidelines state that surgery should be considered for patients with class I obesity BMI 30.0-34.9 kg/m² who experience inadequate control despite oral or injectable medications, noting that all specified BMI thresholds should be lowered by 2.5 kg/m² for patients of Asian descent. Finally, the recommendations emphasize performing operations in high-volume, multidisciplinary centers with long-term post-operative nutritional monitoring and urge healthcare regulators to update reimbursement policies to accommodate surgical diabetes care.

question: What were the main findings of the A Nonlinear Effect of Hyperglycemia and Current Cigarette Smoking Are Major Determinants of the Onset of Microalbuminuria in Type 1 Diabetes.txt study?
passage_1: "A Nonlinear Effect of Hyperglycemia and Current Cigarette Smoking Are Major Determinants of the Onset of Microalbuminuria in Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the temporal and joint effects of glycemic control (measured by HbA1c) and cigarette smoking status on the 4-year incidence of microalbuminuria among 943 young adults with type 1 diabetes from the Natural History of Microalbuminuria Study. The findings demonstrate that microalbuminuria developed at a rate of 3.3 per 100 person-years, with recent HbA1c levels (from the 1st and 2nd years preceding onset) serving as a stronger predictor of risk than older or cumulative 4-year measurements, indicating an attenuation of the impact of past hyperglycemia over time. The study identified a significant nonlinear relationship between HbA1c and microalbuminuria risk, showing a markedly steeper increase in risk once HbA1c exceeds 8%, a risk enhancement that is further magnified among current cigarette smokers (who experienced an incidence rate of 7.9 per 100 person-years compared to 1.8 for past smokers and 2.2 for never-smokers). While no explicit clinical guidelines or recommendations are formally established in the text, the authors conclude that patients with type 1 diabetes who smoke and maintain HbA1c levels above 8% face the highest risk for developing microalbuminuria.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.
passage_3: "Prevalence of Tobacco Use and Association between Cardiometabolic Risk Factors and Cigarette Smoking in Youth with Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus" evaluates the prevalence of tobacco use and its association with cardiometabolic risk factors among youth aged 10 to 22 years with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus using data from the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study. The findings demonstrate that tobacco use is prevalent in this population, increasing significantly with age and reaching 34.0% in youth ≥20 years with type 1 diabetes and 40.3% in those with type 2 diabetes, with higher smoking rates among youth from lower-income families (<$50,000). Furthermore, current cigarette smoking in youth with type 1 diabetes was significantly associated with higher odds of high triglyceride levels and physical inactivity, alongside less favorable overall cardiometabolic risk profiles across both diabetes types. Despite these risks, less than half of younger participants (aged 10–14 years) reported ever receiving counseling from a healthcare provider to avoid or quit smoking. Based on these observations, the paper recommends that aggressive tobacco prevention and smoking cessation programs be made a high priority in clinical care to prevent or delay the onset of cardiovascular disease in youth with diabetes mellitus.

passage_1: "A population-based study of the risk of diabetic retinopathy in patients with type 1 diabetes and celiac disease" reports that celiac disease (CD) is associated with type 1 diabetes (T1D). In the current study, we examined whether CD affects the risk of diabetic retinopathy (DRP) in patients with T1D. This was a population-based cohort study. Through the Swedish National Patient Register, we identified 41,566 patients diagnosed with diabetes in 1964–2009 and who were ≤30 years of age at diagnosis. CD was defined as having villous atrophy (Marsh stage 3) according to small intestinal biopsies performed between 1969 and 2008, with biopsy reports obtained from Sweden’s 28 pathology departments. During follow-up, 947 T1D patients had a diagnosis of CD. The findings indicate that physical exercise negatively impacts sensor accuracy, causing sensors to consistently overestimate blood glucose levels—a performance drop that was significantly more pronounced during moderate continuous exercise than during interval exercise. Based on these results, the paper recommends maintaining blood glucose within a more "prudent" range (above standard targets) during continuous exercise to account for overestimation and prevent unrecognized hypoglycemia, while highlighting the need for further research across additional types of physical activity.

The findings reveal that CGM sensors generally overestimate capillary blood glucose levels, particularly during low-intensity continuous exercise and low- or high-intensity interval exercise, but demonstrate clinically acceptable overall performance across most conditions except during high-intensity continuous exercise. Based on these results, the paper recommends using CGM to help avoid exercise-induced hypoglycemia during physical activity, but provides the guideline that standard capillary blood glucose monitoring should still be performed alongside CGM during high-intensity exercise to ensure safety and prevent unmanaged glycemic events.

While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

passage_1: Advancing Diabetes Management in Adolescents: Comparative Effectiveness of Mobile Self-Monitoring Blood Glucose Technology and Family-Centered Goal Setting evaluates three strategies—a health information technology (HIT)-enhanced blood glucose meter that shares real-time data and allows text messaging, a clinic-based family-centered goal setting intervention using motivational interviewing, and a combined approach of both—to improve self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) and glycemic control (HbA1c) in adolescents aged 12–18 with type 1 diabetes over a 6-month period. The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.

The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. question: What were the main findings of the Alterations in White Matter Structure in Young Children With Type 1 Diabetes.txt study?
passage_1: The study Alterations in White Matter Structure in Young Children With Type 1 Diabetes evaluates whether type 1 diabetes affects white matter brain structure in young children (ages 4 to <10 years) by utilizing diffusion tensor imaging to analyze axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and fractional anisotropy in relation to continuous glucose monitoring metrics, glycemic history, and cognitive function. Results demonstrate that young children with type 1 diabetes exhibit widespread reductions in axial diffusivity across multiple brain regions compared to healthy controls, with microstructural changes significantly driven by chronic hyperglycemia—including elevated HbA1c levels and prolonged glucose elevations above 180, 250, and 300 mg/dL—as well as high glucose variability. Higher blood glucose metrics and erratic fluctuations correspond with decreased fractional anisotropy and increased radial diffusivity, pointing to altered myelination and axonal integrity, whereas hypoglycemic events and severe hypoglycemic seizures show no significant association with white matter structural alterations. Furthermore, fractional anisotropy levels directly correlate with Full-Scale IQ in pediatric diabetes patients, confirming the functional relevance of these white matter changes during early neurodevelopment. While the findings do not establish direct clinical practice guidelines, the clear clinical recommendation for treating pediatric type 1 diabetes is to reorient management strategies toward minimizing chronic hyperglycemia and smoothing out sharp glucose fluctuations rather than focusing predominantly on avoiding hypoglycemia, utilizing continuous glucose monitoring to actively suppress high blood sugar spikes and safeguard early brain development and cognitive potential.
passage_2: The study Neurological Consequences of Diabetic Ketoacidosis at Initial Presentation of Type 1 Diabetes in a Prospective Cohort Study of Children evaluates the acute and medium-term impacts of new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) on brain morphology and cognitive function in children newly diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes. By assessing children aged 6 to 18 years at baseline, day 5, day 28, and 6 months using MRI, MRS, and cognitive testing, the study highlights how DKA alters cerebral structure and neurocognitive performance even without the presence of severe clinical cerebral edema. The findings reveal that children presenting with DKA experience significant changes in white and gray matter structures, including higher total white matter volume and increased mean diffusivity in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes at presentation, alongside reduced total cortical gray matter volume and lower levels of N-acetylaspartate in the frontal gray matter and basal ganglia. Although acute structural and volume changes resolved over time, DKA presentation was associated with persistent adverse functional outcomes at the 6-month follow-up, specifically lower delayed memory recall, poorer sustained and divided attention, and reduced baseline mental state scores. Furthermore, lower blood pH at presentation and younger age were identified as key predictors of both structural brain changes and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. The recommendations and guidelines stemming from this study emphasize the critical need to view DKA-related brain injury along a continuous spectrum rather than as an isolated risk limited to overt cerebral edema. Clinicians and healthcare providers are urged to prioritize early detection and prompt intervention for Type 1 Diabetes in pediatric patients to prevent initial DKA episodes entirely, thereby protecting vulnerable developing brain tissue.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. The review finds that while early evidence of safety and efficacy exists for gastric bypass and laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding, current evidence remains insufficient to definitively determine which specific WLS procedures are optimal for adolescents; however, mature adolescent WLS can reduce the risk of early mortality and morbidity from obesity-related diseases. The study recommends modifying patient selection criteria to include adolescents with a BMI ≥ 35 who have specific obesity-related comorbidities showing clear evidence of short-term morbidity (such as type 2 diabetes, severe steatohepatitis, pseudotumor cerebri, or moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea), as well as considering WLS for adolescents with extreme obesity (BMI ≥ 40) and other comorbidities associated with long-term risks. Furthermore, key guidelines emphasized for ensuring patient safety include establishing carefully designed patient selection criteria, conducting multidisciplinary evaluations, choosing appropriate procedures, performing thorough screening and management of comorbidities, optimizing long-term compliance, and obtaining age-appropriate, fully informed consent.

question: What were the main findings of the Bone Health in Children With Celiac Disease Assessed by Dual X Ray Absorptiometry Effect of Gluten Free Diet and Predictive Value of Serum Biochemical Indices.txt study?
passage_1: "Bone health in children with celiac disease assessed by dual x-ray absorptiometry: effect of gluten-free diet and predictive value of serum biochemical indices" aimed to assess bone status and the effect of gluten-free diet (GFD) in children with celiac disease (CD), and to evaluate the predictive value of standard serum biochemical indices in the diagnosis of bone mineral density (BMD) disturbances. Forty-five children at the time of diagnosis of CD (group A, 77.8% girls) and 36 children receiving GFD for >2 years (group B, 75% girls) were included. Sixteen children in group A were reexamined 12 months after initiation of GFD. Serum measurements of biochemical bone health indices and BMD, assessed by dual x-ray absorptiometry, were obtained. Patients after 1 year of receiving GFD had higher BMD z scores compared with baseline (−1.45 ± 0.28 vs −0.61 ± 0.25, respectively, P = 0.004). BMD z scores were significantly lower than expected for the normal population, after 1 (P = 0.03) or at least 2 (P < 0.001) years of receiving GFD. In group B, BMD z score was positively correlated with 25-hydroxy vitamin D levels (P = 0.009). In the repeated measurements group, 25-hydroxy vitamin D differed between pre- and post-GFD (P = 0.018). No biochemical index was capable of predicting an abnormal BMD z score (receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, all of the areas under the curve <0.66). We concluded that GFD has a beneficial effect on bone health. Two years receiving diet do not ensure normalization. Biochemical markers are not indicative of BMD disturbances. Dual x-ray absorptiometry should be included in the standard management of children with CD.
passage_2: "Celiac disease in children with type 1 diabetes varies around the world: an international, cross-sectional study of 57 375 patients from the SWEET registry" reports that children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at much higher risk of developing celiac disease (CD) than the general population. The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). Further, they had lower glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in Europe and North America/Canada; lower body mass index (BMI)-SD score (BMI-SDS) in southern Europe, North America, and Canada; In most regions daily insulin dose was lower, height-SDS was lower, and the percentage of insulin pump users was higher in children with T1D and CD. We concluded that the prevalence and the anthropometric and metabolic consequences of CD in children with T1D differ around the world.
passage_3: "Sex- and age-dependent effects of celiac disease on growth and weight gain in children with type 1 diabetes: analysis of the Type 1 Diabetes Exchange Clinic Registry" reports that celiac disease (CD) is common in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and effects of CD on growth in children with T1D remain unclear. We analyzed heights, weights, and body mass index (BMI) in 215 matched pediatric CD/control pairs in the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry. CD was defined by a clinic-reported diagnosis and positive celiac serology (n = 80) and/or positive small bowel biopsy (n = 135). Cases and controls were matched by age (mean: 14 years), diabetes duration (median: 7 years), sex (57% female), and clinic site. There were 5569 height/weight measurements. Gluten was restricted for varying periods of time in 61% of females and 51% of males with CD. Females with CD were shorter than female controls at all ages (P = 0.01). Weight z-scores were initially lower in preschool females with CD but similar to controls by middle childhood. Males with CD were initially shorter but adult heights were similar. Height in both sexes and weight in males were lower in CD participants diagnosed at younger age. Growth in T1D children with biopsy-proven CD, 76% of them were gluten-restricted, was comparable to that of T1D controls. We concluded that concurrent CD impairs linear growth in T1D females at all stages of development and in young T1D males. Young females with CD have lower weights, but both sexes have similar weights by middle childhood. Children younger at CD onset remain shorter throughout childhood; males younger at CD onset have persistently lower weights. Long-term gluten restriction may restore weight gain and linear growth in children with CD and T1D.

passage_1: "Clinical and Psychological Course of Diabetes From Adolescence to Young Adulthood" evaluates the longitudinal clinical and psychological progress of 76 adolescents with type 1 diabetes over an 8-year period into young adulthood to determine the relationship between adolescent psychological state and later diabetic outcomes. The study's key findings reveal that glycemic control peaked and worsened during late adolescence—particularly among female participants, who reached an average HbA1c of 11.1% at ages 18–19—and that the proportion of overweight individuals (BMI >25.0 kg/m2) increased significantly from 21% to 54% in females and 2% to 28% in males. Furthermore, serious microvascular complications or hypertension developed in 25% of male and 38% of female participants, strongly correlating with higher mean HbA1c levels, while adolescent behavioral problems were identified as significant predictors of poorer subsequent glycemic control over the 8-year study period.
passage_2: The “Characteristics of adolescents and youth with recent-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY cohort at baseline” evaluates the baseline demographic, clinical, medical history, and biochemical characteristics of 704 American adolescents and youth aged 10 to 17 years who were diagnosed with recent-onset type 2 diabetes for less than two years and had a body mass index at or above the 85th percentile. The findings reveal that the participant group was predominantly female (64.9%), had a mean age of 14.0 years, and consisted mostly of racial and ethnic minority populations, including 41.1% Hispanic and 31.5% non-Hispanic Black youth, with 89.4% having a family history of diabetes and significant socioeconomic challenges such as 41.5% residing in households earning less than $25,000 annually. Furthermore, clinical and biochemical comorbidities were highly prevalent within two years of diagnosis, including low high-density lipoprotein levels in 79.8%, blood pressure at or above the 90th percentile in 26.3%, microalbuminuria in 13.0%, and elevated triglycerides in 10.2% of participants. The study does not explicitly provide formal clinical practice guidelines or recommendations, but it emphasizes that youth-onset type 2 diabetes presents with substantial risk factors and metabolic abnormalities early in the course of the disease.
passage_3: The study “Screening eye exams in youth with type 1 diabetes under 18 years of age: once may be enough?” evaluates the optimal frequency and necessity of eye screening examinations in pediatric patients under 18 years of age with type 1 diabetes, drawing on long-term data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) research group. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

question: What were the main findings of the Developmental Changes in the Roles of Patients and Families in Type 1 Diabetes Management.txt study?
passage_1: The study Developmental Changes in the Roles of Patients and Families in Type 1 Diabetes Management evaluates the evolving division of daily self-care responsibilities between young patients with Type 1 Diabetes and their families across early childhood, middle childhood, and adolescence. The findings reveal that despite modern therapeutic advances like continuous glucose monitors and insulin pumps, daily self-care burdens remain high and glycemic control frequently deteriorates—particularly during adolescence due to pubertal insulin resistance and shifting social priorities. Crucially, the authors note that prematurely transferring diabetes management tasks to maturing youth leads to poorer treatment adherence and compromised metabolic outcomes, whereas ongoing parental involvement, strong youth self-efficacy, and constructive family collaboration consistently associate with better blood glucose monitoring, lower family conflict, and enhanced quality of life. To optimize care across these developmental stages, recommendations and guidelines advise parents to completely manage complex care tasks during early childhood (ages 0–5) using parent-focused behavioral strategies to navigate unpredictable eating, acute illnesses, and parental stress. For middle childhood (ages 6–12), guidelines emphasize establishing a structured "family teamwork" model that teaches basic self-care skills while maintaining active parental supervision and close coordination with school nurses. For adolescence (ages 13–18), recommendations focus on renegotiating roles to support gradual autonomy, building adolescent self-efficacy, and minimizing family conflict, while leveraging multidisciplinary healthcare support and modern technology platforms, such as virtual consultations connecting clinics, families, and school personnel, to ensure sustained adherence and a smooth transition to independent self-management.
passage_2: The American Diabetes Association position statement on Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents emphasizes that pediatric-onset diabetes requires distinct clinical strategies because children are not simply small adults. The disease differs significantly from adult diabetes in its epidemiology, pathophysiology, developmental impact, and response to therapy, meaning care must continuously adapt to match a child's evolving growth stages. The statement outlines a standardized three-stage continuum for disease progression, starting with Stage 1 (presymptomatic with multiple islet autoantibodies and normoglycemia), moving to Stage 2 (presymptomatic with autoantibodies and dysglycemia), and concluding with Stage 3 (symptomatic clinical onset due to insulin deficiency). To manage the condition effectively, diagnosis must be pursued expeditiously to prevent rapid clinical deterioration and diabetic ketoacidosis. Clinicians are advised to differentiate Type 1 diabetes from Type 2, monogenic forms, and atypical presentations using autoantibody panels, family history, and C-peptide testing, while consulting pediatric endocrinologists in ambiguous situations such as stress hyperglycemia. For blood glucose management, the guidelines strongly recommend intensive insulin regimens delivered via multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pumps). Across pediatric age groups, the recommended target A1C level is set at under 7.5%, though this should be tailored based on individual risks like hypoglycemia. Finally, comprehensive care requires monitoring blood glucose multiple times daily, leveraging continuous glucose monitoring systems, and testing blood ketones during acute illness or unexpected hyperglycemia.
passage_3: The study titled Type 1 Diabetes Through the Life Span: A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the global and domestic incidence, diagnostic challenges, and comprehensive management strategies for type 1 diabetes across all age groups. It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.

passage_1: "Dietary Protein Requirements in Children: Methods for Consideration" evaluates the current methodologies used to determine dietary protein recommendations in children, assessing the limitations of traditional nitrogen balance studies alongside newer approaches such as the indicator amino acid oxidation (IAAO) technique, 15N end-product method, virtual biopsy approach, and 2H3-creatine dilution method, while also examining physical activity as a potential modifier of these needs. The authors find that standard nitrogen balance techniques systematically underestimate protein requirements due to methodological errors, whereas alternative stable isotope methods (like IAAO) suggest actual requirements may be up to 60% higher than existing guidelines. Furthermore, evidence indicates that engaging in moderate-to-high levels of physical activity increases lean body mass and protein turnover, likely elevating protein needs to support exercise adaptations and tissue deposition; however, existing research remains insufficient to establish separate guidelines based on activity levels. The paper notes that current Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) recommend 0.95 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for children aged 4–13 years and 0.85 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for ages 14–18 years based on nitrogen balance, concluding that while available data are not yet robust enough to officially overturn these baseline standards, further rigorous research using advanced tracer techniques is urgently needed to accurately define age- and activity-specific protein requirements.
passage_2: The study Impact of dietary protein on postprandial glycaemic control and insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review determines the impact of dietary protein on postprandial blood glucose levels and mealtime insulin requirements in individuals with Type 1 diabetes. Findings indicate that protein consumed alone does not exhibit a significant glycaemic effect until doses reach ≥75 g, whereas within a carbohydrate-containing meal, as little as ≥12.5 g of protein affects postprandial glucose. The timing of this glucose-raising effect ranges from 90 to 240 minutes, and combining fat with a high-protein meal further enhances the postprandial glycaemic response and increases total insulin requirements. Based on these insights, recommendations and guidelines advise that dietary protein must be explicitly taken into account alongside carbohydrates when calculating mealtime insulin doses, emphasizing the need for modified, multi-macronutrient insulin dosing strategies to prevent postprandial hyperglycaemia.
passage_3: The study "Impact of dietary protein on postprandial glycaemic control and insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" evaluates the glycemic impact of dietary protein and the corresponding insulin requirements for individuals living with Type 1 diabetes. By synthesizing evidence from a systematic literature search across biomedical databases, the review highlights that dietary protein significantly contributes to postprandial glycemic excursions alongside carbohydrates, leading to delayed hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the paper discusses recommendations and clinical guidelines to consider dietary protein composition—not just carbohydrate content alone—when calculating mealtime insulin doses to improve overall postprandial glycemic control.

The study found that empagliflozin provided a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in HbA1c baseline levels compared to placebo (-0.84%, p=0.012), whereas linagliptin did not show a statistically significant reduction (-0.34%, p=0.29). Hypoglycemia was the most frequently reported adverse event, with higher rates observed in active treatment groups, though no severe hypoglycemia cases occurred. Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). question: What were the long-term outcomes beyond the study period in the Evaluation of the possible impact of the fear of hypoglycemia on diabetes management in children.txt cross-sectional study?
passage_1: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.
passage_2: "Transfer from pediatric to adult health care: effects on diabetes outcomes" evaluates the impact of transitioning from pediatric to adult diabetes care on emerging adults with type 1 diabetes, focusing on outcomes such as diabetes care visit attendance, glycemic control, and acute diabetes-related complications while assessing the methodological strength of existing observational and interventional studies. The paper's findings indicate that while observational studies often report a decline in diabetes care visit frequency alongside an improvement or no change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) after transfer, these results are heavily limited by methodological flaws, including incomplete data, high dropout rates among patients who drop out of follow-up, lack of appropriate comparison groups, and confounding physical and psychosocial maturation. Furthermore, studies tracking patients who left the pediatric health system for a broad array of adult providers found deterioration in glycemic control compared to peers remaining in pediatric care, and structured transition interventions showed temporary benefits in clinic attendance or HbA1c that were often not sustained long-term. Regarding recommendations and guidelines, the paper does not propose new clinical guidelines or structured transition protocols; instead, it highlights a critical lack of methodologically strong empirical evidence—noting that most current recommendations are based on expert consensus or clinical experience—and emphasizes that future research must address these shortcomings by utilizing proper comparison groups, tracking patients across diverse adult care settings, and accounting for patient attrition to properly guide clinicians and improve emerging adult care.
passage_3: The study Evaluation of the possible impact of the fear of hypoglycemia on diabetes management in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus and their parents: a cross-sectional study evaluates the association between self-reported fear of hypoglycemia (FoH) in 100 Greek children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and their parents using the Hypoglycemia Fear Survey (HFS), alongside demographic and clinical factors such as age, T1DM duration, recent HbA1c levels, treatment mode, and hypoglycemic event frequency. The findings demonstrate that parents experience significantly higher levels of FoH across all subscales compared to their children, while factors like age, diabetes duration, HbA1c, and treatment mode showed no overall significant correlation with HFS scores, though parents of children with HbA1c > 7.0% exhibited higher behavior and total fear scores. Based on these results, the paper recommends that healthcare providers routinely screen for parental FoH and focus on supportive intervention strategies to alleviate their psychological burden and optimize childhood diabetes management.

Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

passage_2: "Genetics of type 1 diabetes" reports that type 1 diabetes, a multifactorial disease with a strong genetic component, is caused by the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β cells. The major susceptibility locus maps to the HLA class II genes at 6p21, although more than 40 non-HLA susceptibility gene markers have been confirmed. Although HLA class II alleles account for up to 30%–50% of genetic type 1 diabetes risk, multiple non-MHC loci contribute to disease risk with smaller effects. These include the insulin, PTPN22, CTLA4, IL2RA, IFIH1, and other recently discovered loci. Genomewide association studies performed with high-density single-nucleotide–polymorphism genotyping platforms have provided evidence for a number of novel loci, although fine mapping and characterization of these new regions remain to be performed. Children born with the high-risk genotype HLADR3/4-DQ8 comprise almost 50% of children who develop antiislet autoimmunity by the age of 5 years. Genetic risk for type 1 diabetes can be further stratified by selection of children with susceptible genotypes at other diabetes genes, by selection of children with a multiple family history of diabetes, and/or by selection of relatives that are HLA identical to the proband. Children with the HLA-risk genotypes DR3/4-DQ8 or DR4/DR4 who have a family history of type 1 diabetes have more than a 1 in 5 risk for developing islet autoantibodies during childhood, and children with the same HLA-risk genotype but no family history have approximately a 1 in 20 risk. Determining extreme genetic risk is a prerequisite for the implementation of primary prevention trials, which are now underway for relatives of individuals with type 1 diabetes.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. passage_1: The position statement titled Glucose management for exercise using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and intermittently scanned CGM (isCGM) systems in type 1 diabetes evaluates the efficacy, accuracy, and practical clinical application of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and intermittently scanned CGM (isCGM) systems around exercise (before, during, and after) in individuals with type 1 diabetes across different age groups and activity levels. The paper finds that while CGM and isCGM technologies significantly reduce time spent in hypoglycemia and improve overall glycemic control, exercise introduces potential sensor inaccuracies and increased lag time (up to 12–24 minutes or longer) between interstitial and blood glucose levels, yielding an overall mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of approximately 13.63% across exercise types. Based on these findings, the paper recommends tailored glucose target thresholds for initiating carbohydrate consumption and exercise—differentiated by exercise intensity, individual hypoglycemia risk, and age—and provides guidelines on optimizing sensor alert settings (e.g., setting lower hypoglycemia alert thresholds up to 5.6 mmol/L / 100 mg/dL at exercise onset to offset sensor lag), using trend arrows to adjust carbohydrate intake or insulin delivery, and performing confirmatory fingerstick blood glucose tests whenever sensor readings conflict with physical symptoms.

The findings reveal that closed-loop systems moderately improved overall time in range during exercise compared to standard of care with an absolute mean difference of 6.18%, with a particularly pronounced and significant benefit in children and adolescents (absolute mean difference of 9.46%) compared to adults (absolute mean difference of 1.07%). Additionally, physical exercise performed on a cycle ergometer demonstrated beneficial effects of closed-loop systems on time in range (mean difference of 12.34%), whereas treadmill exercise and skiing sessions did not show a statistically significant difference. The authors note recommendations highlighting the importance of physical activity for health benefits and mention position statement guidelines concerning glycemic management around exercise—pointing out that continuous glucose monitor accuracy can deteriorate during acute exercise due to physiological lag time between interstitial and blood glucose—and conclude that while closed-loop systems effectively support glycemic control during exercise, further advancement in sensor technology and algorithms is needed to manage rapid glucose fluctuations.

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). passage_1: Insulin strategies for dietary fat and protein in type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the efficacy of various insulin dosing and delivery strategies used to manage postprandial glycaemia following meals high in fat and protein in individuals living with type 1 diabetes. Synthesizing data from 18 randomized controlled trials published between 1995 and 2021, the paper finds that administering additional insulin—specifically an extra 24% to 75% of the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR)—improves postprandial glucose control, whereas increases below 24% generally offer little glycaemic benefit. The findings also demonstrate that split or combination boluses outperform standard single doses, and administering insulin 15 minutes prior to the meal yields superior postprandial glycaemic outcomes. Based on these insights, the paper provides supportive guidelines and recommendations for managing high-fat and high-protein meals, advising an additional 24% to 75% ICR delivered via a combination bolus with a minimum upfront dose of 60% ICR, administered 15 minutes before eating.

Findings indicate that protein consumed alone does not exhibit a significant glycaemic effect until doses reach ≥75 g, whereas within a carbohydrate-containing meal, as little as ≥12.5 g of protein affects postprandial glucose. The timing of this glucose-raising effect ranges from 90 to 240 minutes, and combining fat with a high-protein meal further enhances the postprandial glycaemic response and increases total insulin requirements. Based on these insights, recommendations and guidelines advise that dietary protein must be explicitly taken into account alongside carbohydrates when calculating mealtime insulin doses, emphasizing the need for modified, multi-macronutrient insulin dosing strategies to prevent postprandial hyperglycaemia.

Across a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, the authors found that cardiorespiratory fitness was significantly lower in youth with T2D (44.5% lower; SMD −1.06) and T1D (10% lower; SMD −0.39) compared to controls, with the deficits in CRF being much larger and more consistent among those with T2D. Based on these findings, the paper highlights an increased risk for future cardiovascular disease-related morbidity in youth with diabetes—particularly those with T2D—and recommends the development of novel behavioral interventions designed to empower affected youth to engage in regular physical activity and improve their cardiorespiratory fitness.

Laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery was performed for 81 adolescents with morbid obesity (13-18 years), while 81 adolescents with obesity-matched by age, sex, and BMI received conventional care. Another comparison group was adults undergoing gastric bypass at the same institution during the same time period. This report addresses the 2-year clinical outcome and five-year surgical adverse event rate. Body weight decreased from 133 kg (SD = 22) at inclusion to 92 kg (SD = 17) after 1 year and was 89 (SD = 18) after 2 years (p < 0·001) representing a 32% (-35 to -30) weight loss after 2 years, corresponding to 76% (-81 to -71) excess weight loss. Weight loss was similar in the adult gastric bypass patients (-31%) while weight gain (+3%) was seen in the conventionally treated obese adolescents. Significant improvement in cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors and inflammation was seen after surgery. The treatment was generally well tolerated and quality of life improved significantly. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. There were surgical complications similar to the adult group, which may be preventable.

The study finds that adolescents receiving gastric bypass achieved a 32% total weight loss (76% excess weight loss) after two years—comparable to the 31% weight loss observed in adults, whereas conventionally treated adolescents gained 3% body weight—alongside marked improvements in cardiovascular risk factors, metabolic health, systemic inflammation, and quality of life. The findings demonstrate that cardiovascular risk factors and dyslipidemia worsened significantly over time across all treatment groups, with overall increases in LDL, triglycerides, apolipoprotein B, non-HDL, hsCRP, homocysteine, and PAI-1, alongside a rise in participants meeting high-risk LDL thresholds from 4.5% to 10.7%. While intensive lifestyle intervention yielded lower triglyceride levels and rosiglitazone co-treatment reduced hsCRP compared to metformin alone, standard glucose-lowering treatments and protocol-driven statin adjustments were generally inadequate to arrest this worsening risk, leading to the paper's main recommendation and guideline implication that standard diabetes treatments are insufficient on their own and that aggressive, dedicated management of dyslipidemia and inflammatory risk factors is critical for youth with type 2 diabetes.
passage_2: The "TODAY Reflects on the Changing Faces of Type 2 Diabetes" study evaluates the efficacy, safety, and longitudinal outcomes of three treatment strategies—metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, and metformin plus intensive lifestyle changes—in maintaining glycemic control among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The paper highlights findings demonstrating that metformin monotherapy achieved durable glycemic control in only about half of the youth, whereas the combination of metformin and rosiglitazone significantly improved glycemic durability due to favorable effects on insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function. Although the treatment approaches were generally safe with primarily gastrointestinal side effects, the study interventions were inadequate to prevent the progression of cardiovascular and renal risk factors, as dyslipidemia, chronic inflammation, hypertension, and microalbuminuria worsened over time regardless of diabetes treatment. Considering projections of up to a fourfold increase in youth type 2 diabetes, the commentary emphasizes the critical recommendation for immediate research, screening, medical interventions, and public policy changes to slow and reverse the growing health and economic burden of adolescent-onset type 2 diabetes.

The study found an overall retinopathy prevalence of 13.7%, with all affected participants exhibiting mild or very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and no cases of macular edema or proliferative disease. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). However, it highlights that interventional evidence regarding CGM's effectiveness in directly improving long-term glycemic control specifically in youth with type 2 diabetes remains very limited. Consequently, the paper recommends conducting rigorous future studies to address these knowledge gaps and establish dedicated guidelines for utilizing advanced glucose monitoring tools to optimize clinical outcomes in this young population facing an aggressive form of the disease.

Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.

The study found that while milk type (breast milk versus formula) strongly influenced dietary and serum cholesterol ester fatty acid compositions at 7 months of age, the 6-month dietary counselling intervention—which successfully altered the children's actual fat intake quality at 13 months—had only a minimal effect on serum cholesterol ester fatty acid levels, as serum compositions in all 13-month-olds closely resembled those of 7-month-old breastfed infants regardless of intervention or previous milk type. The findings demonstrate that tobacco use is prevalent in this population, increasing significantly with age and reaching 34.0% in youth ≥20 years with type 1 diabetes and 40.3% in those with type 2 diabetes, with higher smoking rates among youth from lower-income families (<$50,000). Furthermore, current cigarette smoking in youth with type 1 diabetes was significantly associated with higher odds of high triglyceride levels and physical inactivity, alongside less favorable overall cardiometabolic risk profiles across both diabetes types. Despite these risks, less than half of younger participants (aged 10–14 years) reported ever receiving counseling from a healthcare provider to avoid or quit smoking. Across a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, the authors found that cardiorespiratory fitness was significantly lower in youth with T2D (44.5% lower; SMD −1.06) and T1D (10% lower; SMD −0.39) compared to controls, with the deficits in CRF being much larger and more consistent among those with T2D. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

Based on a single randomized controlled trial involving 50 Australian adolescents over two years, the study found that laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding resulted in a significantly greater mean weight reduction of 34.6 kg (a BMI change of 12.7) compared to a 3.0 kg reduction (a BMI change of 1.3) in the lifestyle intervention group, alongside minor improvements in physical functioning and health perception quality-of-life scores. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. passage_2: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

The findings reveal that closed-loop systems moderately improved overall time in range during exercise compared to standard of care with an absolute mean difference of 6.18%, with a particularly pronounced and significant benefit in children and adolescents (absolute mean difference of 9.46%) compared to adults (absolute mean difference of 1.07%). Additionally, physical exercise performed on a cycle ergometer demonstrated beneficial effects of closed-loop systems on time in range (mean difference of 12.34%), whereas treadmill exercise and skiing sessions did not show a statistically significant difference. The authors note recommendations highlighting the importance of physical activity for health benefits and mention position statement guidelines concerning glycemic management around exercise—pointing out that continuous glucose monitor accuracy can deteriorate during acute exercise due to physiological lag time between interstitial and blood glucose—and conclude that while closed-loop systems effectively support glycemic control during exercise, further advancement in sensor technology and algorithms is needed to manage rapid glucose fluctuations.

question: What were the long-term outcomes beyond the study period in the The American Diabetes Association position statement on Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents.txt position statement?
passage_1: The study titled Type 1 Diabetes Through the Life Span: A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the global and domestic incidence, diagnostic challenges, and comprehensive management strategies for type 1 diabetes across all age groups. It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.
passage_2: The American Diabetes Association position statement on Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents emphasizes that pediatric-onset diabetes requires distinct clinical strategies because children are not simply small adults. The disease differs significantly from adult diabetes in its epidemiology, pathophysiology, developmental impact, and response to therapy, meaning care must continuously adapt to match a child's evolving growth stages. The statement outlines a standardized three-stage continuum for disease progression, starting with Stage 1 (presymptomatic with multiple islet autoantibodies and normoglycemia), moving to Stage 2 (presymptomatic with autoantibodies and dysglycemia), and concluding with Stage 3 (symptomatic clinical onset due to insulin deficiency). To manage the condition effectively, diagnosis must be pursued expeditiously to prevent rapid clinical deterioration and diabetic ketoacidosis. Clinicians are advised to differentiate Type 1 diabetes from Type 2, monogenic forms, and atypical presentations using autoantibody panels, family history, and C-peptide testing, while consulting pediatric endocrinologists in ambiguous situations such as stress hyperglycemia. For blood glucose management, the guidelines strongly recommend intensive insulin regimens delivered via multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pumps). Across pediatric age groups, the recommended target A1C level is set at under 7.5%, though this should be tailored based on individual risks like hypoglycemia. Finally, comprehensive care requires monitoring blood glucose multiple times daily, leveraging continuous glucose monitoring systems, and testing blood ketones during acute illness or unexpected hyperglycemia.
passage_3: The study “Screening eye exams in youth with type 1 diabetes under 18 years of age: once may be enough?” evaluates the optimal frequency and necessity of eye screening examinations in pediatric patients under 18 years of age with type 1 diabetes, drawing on long-term data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) research group. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

The study found that impaired fasting glucose was roughly five times more common at baseline than high-risk A_1c (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but high-risk A1c was more persistent over a two-year period (59.4% persistence vs. 46.9% for impaired fasting glucose). Ultimately, the authors conclude that optimal screening strategies for type 2 diabetes in youth remain unresolved due to these distinct clinical profiles and persistence patterns.

The study found that patients experienced significant overall increases in weight, BMI, and BMI z-scores across 3, 6, and 12 months, with quetiapine associated with the highest weight increases by year one; additionally, leptin and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels rose, free thyroxine levels decreased, and baseline factors such as higher insulin resistance, elevated leptin, or pre-existing overweight/obesity predicted greater weight gain. Based on these findings, the paper highlights that awareness and ongoing monitoring of weight-related and metabolic parameters in young patients are essential to help guide clinical decisions regarding antipsychotic prescriptions.

The findings demonstrate that cardiovascular risk factors and dyslipidemia worsened significantly over time across all treatment groups, with overall increases in LDL, triglycerides, apolipoprotein B, non-HDL, hsCRP, homocysteine, and PAI-1, alongside a rise in participants meeting high-risk LDL thresholds from 4.5% to 10.7%. While intensive lifestyle intervention yielded lower triglyceride levels and rosiglitazone co-treatment reduced hsCRP compared to metformin alone, standard glucose-lowering treatments and protocol-driven statin adjustments were generally inadequate to arrest this worsening risk, leading to the paper's main recommendation and guideline implication that standard diabetes treatments are insufficient on their own and that aggressive, dedicated management of dyslipidemia and inflammatory risk factors is critical for youth with type 2 diabetes.

Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). The guideline finds that pediatric obesity is a major global health concern driven by genetic susceptibilities in a permissive environment, noting that underlying endocrine etiologies are rare and typically accompanied by impaired growth velocity. To diagnose and screen patients, the guidelines recommend using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) BMI percentiles for children aged two and older, while recommending against routine insulin testing or general endocrine labs unless height velocity is reduced. question: What were the main findings of the The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study.txt study?
passage_1: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

In response to concerns regarding the generalizability of their original findings, the authors note that historical clinical trial cohorts remain relevant, address changes in retinal photography methods (such as shifting from seven-field to one- or two-field screening), and emphasize that data-driven, personalized screening intervals offer an effective and cost-saving alternative to universal annual exams without compromising patient care.

The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.

Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

The paper's findings indicate that while observational studies often report a decline in diabetes care visit frequency alongside an improvement or no change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) after transfer, these results are heavily limited by methodological flaws, including incomplete data, high dropout rates among patients who drop out of follow-up, lack of appropriate comparison groups, and confounding physical and psychosocial maturation. Furthermore, studies tracking patients who left the pediatric health system for a broad array of adult providers found deterioration in glycemic control compared to peers remaining in pediatric care, and structured transition interventions showed temporary benefits in clinic attendance or HbA1c that were often not sustained long-term. passage_1: The “Health-Related Quality of Life of Children and Adolescents with Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus” evaluates the associations between demographic and diabetes management variables and the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) among 2,445 children and adolescents aged 8 to 22 years with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus across multiple U.S. study sites. The study found that youth with type 2 diabetes reported significantly lower overall HRQOL compared to those with type 1 diabetes; among participants with type 1 diabetes, worse HRQOL was associated with government-funded insurance, insulin injections versus pump therapy, elevated HbA_1c levels (≥9%), higher rates of comorbidities, and recent emergency department visits or hospitalizations, alongside a significant age-by-sex interaction where HRQOL declined in older girls but improved in older boys. For participants with type 2 diabetes, injecting insulin at least three times daily was associated with better HRQOL, whereas having two or more emergency department visits in the preceding six months was associated with lower HRQOL. The authors recommend that interventions aimed at improving HRQOL in youth with diabetes account for treatment modal differences, complication risks, and gender-specific adjustment patterns across developmental age groups.

The findings indicate that out of 182 participants, 56% transferred to adult care, 15% received no care, and 29% remained in pediatric care, with higher age at diagnosis and longer diabetes duration predicting the departure from pediatric care. passage_1: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
